verses.text: Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made. And he said to the woman, "Did God really say, 'You must not eat from any tree in the garden?'"
The woman answered the serpent, "We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden,
but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God has said, 'You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.'"
"You will not surely die," the serpent told her.
"For God knows that in the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.
And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.
Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and they hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.
But the LORD God called out to the man, "Where are you?"
"I heard Your voice in the garden," he replied, "and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself."
"Who told you that you were naked?" asked the LORD God. "Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?"
And the man answered, "The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it."
Then the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this you have done?" "The serpent deceived me," she replied, "and I ate."

So the LORD God said to the serpent: "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and every beast of the field! On your belly will you go, and dust you will eat, all the days of your life.
And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel."
To the woman He said: "I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth; in pain you will bring forth children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you."

And to Adam He said: "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground because of you; through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.
Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you, and you will eat the plants of the field.
By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread, until you return to the ground— because out of it were you taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return."
And Adam named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living.
And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.
Then the LORD God said, "Behold, the man has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever..."
Therefore the LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.
So He drove out the man and stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Narrative of beginnings (Genesis 1-11): creation, the first family, the flood and the nations, with genealogies
context.audience: Israel, God’s covenant people, learning who their God is, where the world came from and what went wrong with it
context.setting: The serpent, “more crafty than any beast of the field,” asks the woman, “Did God really say…?” (v.1). He tells her, “You will not surely die,” but “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (vv.4-5). She sees that the fruit is good for food and desirable for wisdom, eats, and gives some to her husband, who is with her (v.6). Their eyes are opened, they know they are naked, and they sew fig leaves together (v.7). They hide when they hear the LORD God walking in the garden, and He calls, “Where are you?” (vv.8-9). The man blames the woman, and the woman blames the serpent (vv.12-13). God curses the serpent and promises enmity between its offspring and hers: “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel” (v.15). Childbearing will come with pain, the ground is cursed, and “for dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (vv.16-19). God makes garments of skin for them (v.21) and sends them out of the garden, and cherubim with a flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life (vv.23-24).
context.custom: Serpents were symbols of wisdom, life and danger across the ancient world, and in Egypt the cobra stood on Pharaoh’s crown. There is a play on words: the couple were naked (arummim, 2:25), the serpent was crafty (arum, 3:1). Cherubim, winged guardians, stood beside the thrones and temples of the ancient Near East; Israel later embroidered them on the curtain of the tabernacle and set two of gold over the ark (Exodus 25:18-22; 26:31).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 4 follows the first family outside the garden: Cain kills his brother Abel.
context.timelineBible: Since Irenaeus (about AD 180), Christians have read v.15 as the first promise of the gospel, later called the protoevangelium: a son of the woman would defeat evil. Paul says sin came into the world through one man, and grace through one man, Jesus Christ (Romans 5:12-19); “as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Revelation calls Satan “that ancient serpent” (Revelation 12:9).

translation.meaning: Shrewd, prudent. In Proverbs the same word is praise (‘the prudent’), but here it is cunning used to deceive.
Seed: offspring, descendants. It can mean one descendant or many, a word that runs through all of Genesis.
Winged guardian beings who stand at God’s presence: here at Eden’s gate, later over the ark of the covenant.

gospelParallels.note: Sin entered through one man; grace through one man, Jesus Christ.
The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.
No longer will there be any curse.

otBackground.note: All come from dust, and all return to dust.
Dust will be the serpent’s food.

mapCoords.placeName: Eden (location unknown; Genesis names the Tigris and Euphrates)

overview.summary: The serpent deceives the woman, the man and woman eat the forbidden fruit and hide from God, and God judges them, promises that the woman’s offspring will crush the serpent, clothes them and sends them out of Eden.
overview.settingLine: The garden, and the way out of it.
overview.placeName: Eden (location unknown; Genesis names the Tigris and Euphrates)

history.t: Signs of wisdom, life and danger in the ancient world.
Winged guardians at thrones and temples.

customs.t: The fig has the largest leaves of the land’s trees.

archaeology.t: The rearing cobra on Pharaoh’s crown, a symbol of royal power.
Great winged bulls and lions guarded Assyrian palace gates.

overview.discussion: God’s first words to the hiding couple are a question: “Where are you?” (v.9). Where am I hiding from God right now, and what would it mean to answer Him?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters (1-25 in the app so far). Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham and his family.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

peoplePlaces.d: Eats and gives to her husband

historicalImage.caption: The Fall and Expulsion from the Garden of Eden, by Michelangelo (1509-10), Sistine Chapel. On the left the serpent, a woman from the waist up, coils round the tree; on the right an angel with a sword drives the man and woman out (Genesis 3:6, 23-24).

currentImage.caption: The Anastasis (Resurrection) fresco in the Chora Church, Istanbul (about 1320). Christ, having broken the gates of death, pulls Adam and Eve out of their tombs. Paul: “For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).
